title: Pipeline health
description: One dashboard covering the four signals the assessment names: pipeline health, data freshness, CDC lag and resource usage. Panel order follows the data path, so a reader scans left to right and top to bottom in the direction the data actually moves.

panels.title: CDC lag (heartbeat)
panels.description: Seconds since the last Debezium heartbeat reached ClickHouse. This is connector LIVENESS, measured against a row that is updated on a fixed 10 second timer, not against a business table. Lag measured per business table conflates a stopped connector with a table that simply has not changed: an idle dimension reported 1805 seconds here during testing while nothing was wrong. Thresholds match the CdcPipelineStalled alert exactly, so the panel and the alert cannot disagree.

panels.title: Replication slot: retained WAL
panels.description: WAL bytes the CDC replication slot is holding on the SOURCE database. This is the failure with the worst blast radius in the whole design: an inactive slot retains WAL indefinitely so a consumer that might return can resume, and if none returns the source's disk fills while nothing about the connector looks wrong. The red threshold matches ReplicationSlotRetainingWal; the server independently caps this at max_slot_wal_keep_size=2GB.

panels.title: Change events by operation
panels.description: Events retained in the 30 day immutable log, split by operation. The useful reading is the shape rather than the absolute number: a re-ingest that produced thousands of updates would mean the change-detecting upsert has stopped working and the CDC stream has started describing the scheduler rather than reality.

panels.title: Pipeline health: did data move through every stage
Rows per layer
panels.description: Row counts along the whole path: landing, staging, fact, and the ML feature table. This is the panel that answers the assessment's validate-each-stage question visually. Landing and staging should track each other exactly; the fact table matches staging; the feature table is one row per country and year, so it is deliberately far smaller.

panels.title: Source to warehouse parity
panels.description: Observation rows in ClickHouse as a fraction of rows in PostgreSQL. The single most important correctness number on this dashboard, because dropped events are invisible in every other signal: the connector reports RUNNING, lag stays low, and the warehouse is quietly short. clamp_min on the denominator keeps this readable on a fresh stack instead of showing a divide-by-zero.

panels.title: Quality gates
panels.description: Two counters that should both stay at zero: events quarantined because their primary key could not be attributed to a business entity, and rows the pre-load validation gate rejected. Non-zero is not necessarily an outage, it is a data question, and both are inspectable in raw.cdc_quarantine and ops.ingest_reject.

panels.title: Data freshness: time since last change, per table
panels.description: Informational, and deliberately NOT alerted on by itself. A table with no recent events is usually a table nothing changed in: these are annual statistics, so a flat line here is the normal state. It becomes meaningful only in combination with the CDC lag panel above, which is exactly how the ObservationDataStale alert is written.

panels.title: ClickHouse active parts, and memory
panels.description: Active parts per table is direct evidence for this project's deliberate decision NOT to partition its tables: a flat, low count means the choice is holding. It is also the early warning for too_many_parts, which is an approaching WRITE OUTAGE rather than a performance note, since ClickHouse refuses inserts past 300 parts per partition by default. Memory comes from ClickHouse's native endpoint, so no exporter container is involved.

panels.title: Ingestion outcomes
panels.description: Runs by status, and time since the last success. Answers the question a row count cannot: a full table proves the pipeline worked once, not that it worked today. A rising failed count with a flat success count is the shape of a pipeline that has stopped while its data still looks complete.
